Joseph Campbell at age 82:

In my twenties and thirties and even on into my forties, James Joyce and Thomas Mann were my teachers. I read everything they wrote. Both were writing in terms of what might be called the mythological traditions. Take, for example, the story of Tonio, in Thomas Mann's Tonio Kroger. Tonio's father was a substantial businessman, a major citizen in his hometown. Little Tonio, however, had an artistic temperament, so he moved to Munich and joined a group of literary people who felt themselves above the mere money earners and family men.

So here is Tonio between two poles: his father, who was a good father, responsible and all of that, but who never did the thing he wanted to in all his life -- and, on the other hand, the one who leaves his hometown and becomes a critic of that kind of life. But Tonio found that he really loved these hometown people. And although he thought himself a little superior in an intellectual way to them and could describe them with cutting words, his heart was nevertheless with them.

But when he left to live with the bohemians, he found that they were so disdainful of life that he couldn't stay with them, either. So he left them, and wrote a letter back to someone in the group, saying, "I admire those cold, proud beings who adventure upon the paths of great and daemonic beauty and despise 'mankind'; but I do not envy them. For if anything is capable of making a poet of a literary man, it is my hometown love of the human, the living and ordinary. All warmth derives from this love, all kindness and all humor. Indeed, to me it even seems that this must be that love of which it is written that one may 'speak with the tongues of men and of angels,' and yet, lacking love, be 'as sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal.'"

And then he says, "The writer must be true to truth." And that's a killer, because the only way you can describe a human being truly is by describing his imperfections. The perfect human being is uninteresting -- the Buddha who leaves the world, you know. It is the imperfections of life that are lovable. And when the writer sends a dart of the true word, it hurts. But it goes with love. This is what Mann called "erotic irony," the love for that which you are killing with your cruel, analytical word.

Just something I have been curious of since I started posting on Reddit a few months ago. Does it maybe depend on the time of day it is posted? Or is it just bad luck for the original poster?
Why do reposts sometimes make it to the front page instead of original posts posted a few hours earlier?

I think the first few people to look at a post can have a pretty big impact on it. If the first person to look at a post decides to down vote for whatever reason it can kill the post. Then the same thing gets posted an hour later and happens to get seen by the upvoat happy Voater McUpvoat instead of Negative McDownVoat and it does much better.

It basically comes down to luck. If the repost gets a few upvotes fast it rises from the puddle of new submissions and can get enough attention to rise to the top.

Also sometimes the repost has a "better" title, which is also not to be underestimated.
A post is 49% content and 51% delivery. Sometimes the original just wasn't presented in an appealing way.

I remember a post about Reddit a year (or so) ago stating that it was all about timing. A large number of users are in the US, so the majority of exposure and views were going to happen as people are waking up and going to work, and as people are getting home from work.

If a post starts at those times, it tends to have a better chance of getting upvotes than it would at other times of the day.

Given that most original content creators spend their time analyzing this breakdown, and most reposters live and die by these times, it's not surprising that original content shows up at "off times" and reposters take those rarely-seen posts and repost them at better times, achieving more points.

Back in freshman year of college, I had a pretty severe choking incident which lead me to not being able to eat solid food (or much of any food) for 6 months! I dropped to close to 125lb or less (at 5'11" height) and I barely ate anything for approximately 6 months. It's been 3ish years since then and I've gotten back to eating solid foods again, although I'm still an extremely slow eater. I'm currently up to 135lbs and I'm eating a lot healthier (at times!).

So AMA! Eating disorders aren't always due to low self-image and if you know anyone who is struggling with one (men or women!), please try and encourage them to find help!

Here's the link to National Eating Disorder Association, although if anyone knows of helpful resources I'll update this post.
I wasn't able to eat solid food for 6 months, AMA!

Was your inability to eat due to a physical injury from the choking incident or was it a psychological issue? Your title made me think it was the former but I think after reading your description it sounds like the latter.

If it was a psychological block would you care to explain what would go through your mind when attempting to eat solid or any food. Why was it difficult?

I believe it was primarily psychological but it could have also been physical injury. I had a procedure done to check to make sure there was no damage and mildly expand my esophagus to try and improve my eating ability.

When eating food, my biggest fear was that I'd choke again. I tried to eat solid food after my first incident and felt like I was choking, at which point I started to avoid any sort of solid food. I felt like I couldn't chew the food up right, that it'd slide down my throat at any moment, and it'd get stuck there.

It was weird because when I really started to get better was when I was at a thanksgiving dinner with family and we were eating turkey, mashed potatoes, and lasagna (yeah we're weird, lol).For some reason it clicked and I was able to actually eat more than the potatoes. It was still slow - I couldn't eat more than extremely small bites at a time and I'd only eat maybe half a palm's worth of solid food before I'd stop, but I could eat again. I would favor foods that I could cut into small bites and that weren't overly difficult but over time I worked up to where now I pretty much eat anything except hardcandy. I still eat kinda slow, but it helps me keep from overeating!

What were your favorite "meals" and how did you keep to this regimen for half a year?

I had my wisdom teeth and was told to stay on soft food for a week (or so) and I couldn't make it two days!

My typical meals were essentially tomato soup or blended chicken noodle soup and a super-large shake from a fast food joint. If I wasn't such an ice cream fiend, I probably wouldn't have made it!

A large ice cream shake was like 1k to 1.5k calories, so I was at least getting -some- reasonable amount of calories, even if it wasn't super healthy. I'd also drink stuff like milk or v8 (and sometimes ensures) to try and get something healthy in me. I really wish I learned about soylent at that time, it would have been a godsend. DIY 2k calories a day with all macro and micro nutrients? Hell yes!

And I kept the regiment because I had no other choice. I wasn't able to eat solid food and I was basically just trying to keep from slowly starving to death. I'm lucky that I'm not super active most of the time, but it was an extremely tough time to get through.

One thing that made it easier is that I've always had a sketchy relationship with food. I wouldn't eat much as a kid or I'd just skip meals because I would be reading a book or playing video games. And because I was always a slow eater, I'd just eat less and go do something else. I've always been comfortable with being hungry, which is both a good and bad thing really. On the plus side, my boyfriend certainly appreciates that I keep myself thin! But there's a reason he's the muscle and I'm the brains in our relationship, lol.

Anyway, the basic gist was creamed soups, milkshakes, and occasionally blending chili or weird stuff together. I tried to blend meatloaf into tomato soup and it kinda worked? Although when I started eating again, food tasted so amazing! I forgot how delicious meats could be!

I'm sorry to turn your situation into a joke, but when you said, "soylent" I couldn't think of anything other than Soylent Green... I actually laughed at that point.

I never thought about blended soups. That is actually a REALLY good idea.

Don't stress it, I joke about all the crazy shit that happens to me!

And yeah, soylent was named in reference to soylent green, lol. And the blended soups wasn't bad but what I thought was super surprising was that it's -really- hard to find meals designed to be as calorically dense as possible. In the US, all food manufacturers are looking to minimize calories, not maximize them.
How did you manage to eat solids again?

I talked about this in another comment but it happened in a series of stages.

I tried to talk to a therapist (a college counselor) but they were completely useless. Nice guy, but had NO idea what to try and do so I could actually eat food.

Anyway, I went through a procedure to expand my esophagus and check for any damage from my choking incidents, but that didn't really solve the problem. Eventually I went to thanksgiving dinner with my extended family (I went to college out of state so I was doing thanksgiving with my local relatives) and I expected to mostly eat mashed potatoes and the cranberry sauce. I don't really know what happened but things 'clicked' at dinner. My mom jokes that their thanksgiving dinner cured me, because I started eating into the stuffing and turkey right there! It was awesome! Oh and there was lasagna, which was weird but delicious.

First solid food I ate in -months-. I wasn't completely 'cured', I only ate maybe half a palms worth of solid food + mash potatoes, but it was something! I started to improve my ability to eat more food in a single sitting and eat more complicated food. Originally I'd eat things like stuffing or more bite-sized things that were easy to chew but still somewhat solid.

Eventually I got back to being able to eat pretty much everything and eat a decent sized meal in a semi-reasonable amount of time. It took another 6 months or a year for me to get really comfortable eating without focusing on each bite and making surer I didn't choke to death. I felt like I sorta had to re-learn how to eat and getting comfortable with it again. Now I'm just happy I can eat again! Food is super delicious when you can't eat it for like 6 months, lol.
